L187: @* \[1] Introduction.
L188: This is \eTeX, a program derived from and extending the capabilities of
L189: \TeX, a document compiler intended to produce typesetting of high
L190: quality.
L191: The \PASCAL\ program that follows is the definition of \TeX82, a standard
L192: @:PASCAL}{\PASCAL@>
L193: @!@:TeX82}{\TeX82@>
L194: version of \TeX\ that is designed to be highly portable so that identical output
L195: will be obtainable on a great variety of computers.
L196: The main purpose of the following program is to explain the algorithms of \TeX\
L197: as clearly as possible. As a result, the program will not necessarily be very
L198: efficient when a particular \PASCAL\ compiler has translated it into a
L199: particular machine language. However, the program has been written so that it
L200: can be tuned to run efficiently in a wide variety of operating environments
L201: by making comparatively few changes. Such flexibility is possible because
L202: the documentation that follows is written in the \.{WEB} language, which is
L203: at a higher level than \PASCAL; the preprocessing step that converts \.{WEB}
L204: to \PASCAL\ is able to introduce most of the necessary refinements.
L205: Semi-automatic translation to other languages is also feasible, because the
L206: program below does not make extensive use of features that are peculiar to
L207: \PASCAL.
L208: A large piece of software like \TeX\ has inherent complexity that cannot
L209: be reduced below a certain level of difficulty, although each individual
L210: part is fairly simple by itself. The \.{WEB} language is intended to make
L211: the algorithms as readable as possible, by reflecting the way the
L212: individual program pieces fit together and by providing the
L213: cross-references that connect different parts. Detailed comments about
L214: what is going on, and about why things were done in certain ways, have
L215: been liberally sprinkled throughout the program.  These comments explain
L216: features of the implementation, but they rarely attempt to explain the
L217: \TeX\ language itself, since the reader is supposed to be familiar with
L218: {\sl The \TeX book}.
L219: @.WEB@>
L220: @:TeXbook}{\sl The \TeX book@>
L221: @ The present implementation has a long ancestry, beginning in the summer
L222: of~1977, when Michael~F. Plass and Frank~M. Liang designed and coded
L223: a prototype
L224: @^Plass, Michael Frederick@>
L225: @^Liang, Franklin Mark@>
L226: @^Knuth, Donald Ervin@>
L227: based on some specifications that the author had made in May of that year.
L228: This original proto\TeX\ included macro definitions and elementary
L229: manipulations on boxes and glue, but it did not have line-breaking,
L230: page-breaking, mathematical formulas, alignment routines, error recovery,
L231: or the present semantic nest; furthermore,
L232: it used character lists instead of token lists, so that a control sequence
L233: like \.{\\halign} was represented by a list of seven characters. A
L234: complete version of \TeX\ was designed and coded by the author in late
L235: 1977 and early 1978; that program, like its prototype, was written in the
L236: {\mc SAIL} language, for which an excellent debugging system was
L237: available. Preliminary plans to convert the {\mc SAIL} code into a form
L238: somewhat like the present ``web'' were developed by Luis Trabb~Pardo and
L239: @^Trabb Pardo, Luis Isidoro@>
L240: the author at the beginning of 1979, and a complete implementation was
L241: created by Ignacio~A. Zabala in 1979 and 1980. The \TeX82 program, which
L242: @^Zabala Salelles, Ignacio Andr\'es@>
L243: was written by the author during the latter part of 1981 and the early
L244: part of 1982, also incorporates ideas from the 1979 implementation of
L245: @^Guibas, Leonidas Ioannis@>
L246: @^Sedgewick, Robert@>
L247: @^Wyatt, Douglas Kirk@>
L248: \TeX\ in {\mc MESA} that was written by Leonidas Guibas, Robert Sedgewick,
L249: and Douglas Wyatt at the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center.  Several hundred
L250: refinements were introduced into \TeX82 based on the experiences gained with
L251: the original implementations, so that essentially every part of the system
L252: has been substantially improved. After the appearance of ``Version 0'' in
L253: September 1982, this program benefited greatly from the comments of
L254: many other people, notably David~R. Fuchs and Howard~W. Trickey.
L255: A final revision in September 1989 extended the input character set to
L256: eight-bit codes and introduced the ability to hyphenate words from
L257: different languages, based on some ideas of Michael~J. Ferguson.
L258: @^Fuchs, David Raymond@>
L259: @^Trickey, Howard Wellington@>
L260: @^Ferguson, Michael John@>
L261: No doubt there still is plenty of room for improvement, but the author
L262: is firmly committed to keeping \TeX82 ``frozen'' from now on; stability
L263: and reliability are to be its main virtues.
L264: On the other hand, the \.{WEB} description can be extended without changing
L265: the core of \TeX82 itself, and the program has been designed so that such
L266: extensions are not extremely difficult to make.
L267: The |banner| string defined here should be changed whenever \TeX\
L268: undergoes any modifications, so that it will be clear which version of
L269: \TeX\ might be the guilty party when a problem arises.
L270: @^extensions to \TeX@>
L271: @^system dependencies@>
L272: This program contains code for various features extending \TeX,
L273: therefore this program is called `\eTeX' and not
L274: `\TeX'; the official name `\TeX' by itself is reserved
L275: for software systems that are fully compatible with each other.
L276: A special test suite called the ``\.{TRIP} test'' is available for
L277: helping to determine whether a particular implementation deserves to be
L278: known as `\TeX' [cf.~Stanford Computer Science report CS1027,
L279: November 1984].
L280: A similar test suite called the ``\.{e-TRIP} test'' is available for
L281: helping to determine whether a particular implementation deserves to be
L282: known as `\eTeX'.

L306: @ Different \PASCAL s have slightly different conventions, and the present
L307: @!@:PASCAL H}{\ph@>
L308: program expresses \TeX\ in terms of the \PASCAL\ that was
L309: available to the author in 1982. Constructions that apply to
L310: this particular compiler, which we shall call \ph, should help the
L311: reader see how to make an appropriate interface for other systems
L312: if necessary. (\ph\ is Charles Hedrick's modification of a compiler
L313: @^Hedrick, Charles Locke@>
L314: for the DECsystem-10 that was originally developed at the University of
L315: Hamburg; cf.\ {\sl Software---Practice and Experience \bf6} (1976),
L316: 29--42. The \TeX\ program below is intended to be adaptable, without
L317: extensive changes, to most other versions of \PASCAL, so it does not fully
L318: use the admirable features of \ph. Indeed, a conscious effort has been
L319: made here to avoid using several idiosyncratic features of standard
L320: \PASCAL\ itself, so that most of the code can be translated mechanically
L321: into other high-level languages. For example, the `\&{with}' and `\\{new}'
L322: features are not used, nor are pointer types, set types, or enumerated
L323: scalar types; there are no `\&{var}' parameters, except in the case of files
L324: --- \eTeX, however, does use `\&{var}' parameters for the |reverse| function;
L325: there are no tag fields on variant records; there are no assignments
L326: |real:=integer|; no procedures are declared local to other procedures.)
L327: The portions of this program that involve system-dependent code, where
L328: changes might be necessary because of differences between \PASCAL\ compilers
L329: and/or differences between
L330: operating systems, can be identified by looking at the sections whose
L331: numbers are listed under `system dependencies' in the index. Furthermore,
L332: the index entries for `dirty \PASCAL' list all places where the restrictions
L333: of \PASCAL\ have not been followed perfectly, for one reason or another.
L334: @!@^system dependencies@>
L335: @!@^dirty \PASCAL@>
L336: Incidentally, \PASCAL's standard |round| function can be problematical,
L337: because it disagrees with the IEEE floating-point standard.
L338: Many implementors have
L339: therefore chosen to substitute their own home-grown rounding procedure.
L340: @ The program begins with a normal \PASCAL\ program heading, whose
L341: components will be filled in later, using the conventions of \.{WEB}.
L342: @.WEB@>
L343: For example, the portion of the program called `\X\glob:Global
L344: variables\X' below will be replaced by a sequence of variable declarations

L349: sections \gglob, \dots,'' also make it possible to look at the set of
L350: all global variables, if desired.  Similar remarks apply to the other

L352: Actually the heading shown here is not quite normal: The |program| line

L394: @ Some of the code below is intended to be used only when diagnosing the
L395: strange behavior that sometimes occurs when \TeX\ is being installed or
L396: when system wizards are fooling around with \TeX\ without quite knowing
L397: what they are doing. Such code will not normally be compiled; it is
L398: delimited by the codewords `$|debug|\ldots|gubed|$', with apologies
L399: to people who wish to preserve the purity of English.
L400: Similarly, there is some conditional code delimited by
L401: `$|stat|\ldots|tats|$' that is intended for use when statistics are to be
L402: kept about \TeX's memory usage.  The |stat| $\ldots$ |tats| code also
L403: implements diagnostic information for \.{\\tracingparagraphs},
L404: \.{\\tracingpages}, and \.{\\tracingrestores}.
L405: @^debugging@>
L406: @d debug==@{ {change this to `$\\{debug}\equiv\null$' when debugging}
L407: @d gubed==@t@>@} {change this to `$\\{gubed}\equiv\null$' when debugging}
L408: @f debug==begin
L409: @f gubed==end
L410: @#
L411: @d stat==@{ {change this to `$\\{stat}\equiv\null$' when gathering
L412:   usage statistics}
L413: @d tats==@t@>@} {change this to `$\\{tats}\equiv\null$' when gathering
L414:   usage statistics}
L415: @f stat==begin
L416: @f tats==end
L417: @ This program has two important variations: (1) There is a long and slow
L418: version called \.{INITEX}, which does the extra calculations needed to
L419: @.INITEX@>
L420: initialize \TeX's internal tables; and (2)~there is a shorter and faster
L421: production version, which cuts the initialization to a bare minimum.
L422: Parts of the program that are needed in (1) but not in (2) are delimited by
L423: the codewords `$|init|\ldots|tini|$'.
